items.title: JPA vs Hibernate vs Spring Data JPA vs Spring JDBC
items.context: JPA is a specification for mapping Java objects to relational tables. Hibernate is the most popular implementation of that specification. Spring Data JPA sits on top of JPA and removes boilerplate via repository interfaces. Spring JDBC is lower-level — more control, more manual code, no ORM mapping.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a specification rather than a concrete implementation?
choices: Spring Data JPA
Hibernate
Spring JDBC
JPA
questions.explanation: JPA (Java Persistence API) defines the interfaces and annotations; Hibernate is a popular concrete implementation of that spec.

questions.prompt: What does Spring Data JPA primarily add on top of plain JPA?
choices: Built-in caching that replaces the database
Repository interfaces that eliminate boilerplate CRUD and query code
Automatic UI generation
A completely different query language
questions.explanation: Spring Data JPA lets you declare an interface (e.g. extending JpaRepository) and get CRUD plus derived-query methods for free, without writing implementation code.

items.title: Spring Data repositories
items.context: Extending JpaRepository<Entity, IdType> gives you save/findById/findAll/delete and more, plus the ability to add custom finder methods just by declaring their method signature (e.g. findByLastName).

questions.prompt: What do you get for free by extending JpaRepository<User, Long>?
choices: Automatic database schema design
Nothing until you write the implementation yourself
Standard CRUD operations (save, findById, findAll, delete, etc.) with no implementation code
A REST controller for User
questions.explanation: Spring Data JPA generates the implementation for you at runtime — you only declare the interface, and common CRUD operations (plus derived query methods) just work.

items.title: Transactions
items.context: @Transactional declaratively wraps a method in a database transaction — if it completes normally the transaction commits; if an unchecked exception propagates out, it rolls back by default.

questions.prompt: By default, what causes a @Transactional method's transaction to roll back?
choices: Any return value that is null
An unchecked (runtime) exception propagating out of the method
The method taking longer than 1 second
Nothing — @Transactional never rolls back automatically
questions.explanation: Spring's default rollback rule is: roll back on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and its subclasses), and commit otherwise. Checked exceptions need explicit rollback rules to trigger a rollback.

items.title: Entity mapping basics
items.context: A JPA entity is a plain class annotated @Entity, mapped to a table. @Id marks its primary key field, and @Column, @Table, etc. let you customize the mapping when it doesn't match Java naming conventions.

questions.prompt: Which annotation marks a plain Java class as a JPA-managed entity mapped to a database table?
choices: @Table
@Entity
@Repository
@Bean
questions.explanation: @Entity is what tells JPA/Hibernate that instances of this class should be persisted as rows in a corresponding table.

questions.prompt: Which annotation marks the field that serves as an entity's primary key?
choices: @Id
@Column(primary = true)
@PrimaryKey
@Key
questions.explanation: @Id designates the primary key field of an entity; it's often paired with @GeneratedValue to have the database or JPA provider generate its value.

items.title: Fetch types: lazy vs eager
items.context: JPA associations can be fetched lazily (loaded only when accessed — the default for @OneToMany/@ManyToMany) or eagerly (loaded immediately with the owning entity — the default for @ManyToOne/@OneToOne). Careless lazy loading across a loop is the classic cause of the N+1 query problem.

questions.prompt: What is the default fetch type for a @OneToMany association in JPA?
choices: It has no default, you must always specify one
LAZY
Fetch type only applies to @ManyToOne
EAGER
questions.explanation: Collections (@OneToMany, @ManyToMany) default to LAZY loading — the related entities are only fetched when the collection is actually accessed.

questions.prompt: Iterating over a list of parent entities and accessing each one's lazily-loaded collection triggers a separate query per parent. What problem is this?
choices: A CSRF vulnerability
Cache eviction
The N+1 query problem
Deadlock
questions.explanation: This is the classic N+1 problem: one query to fetch the N parents, then one additional query per parent to lazily fetch its collection — commonly fixed with a JOIN FETCH or an entity graph.

items.title: Derived query methods & JPQL
items.context: Spring Data JPA can generate a query just from a repository method's name, like findByLastNameAndAgeGreaterThan(...). For anything more complex, JPQL (Java Persistence Query Language) lets you write SQL-like queries that operate on entities and their fields rather than raw tables and columns.

questions.prompt: Given a repository method named findByLastName(String lastName), how does Spring Data JPA know what query to run?
choices: It always runs a full table scan
It requires a manually written implementation
It parses the method name itself to derive the query at runtime
It only works if you also write raw SQL
questions.explanation: Spring Data JPA parses conventions in the method name (findBy, And, GreaterThan, ...) to build the corresponding query automatically, no implementation code needed.

questions.prompt: What does JPQL operate on, in contrast to raw SQL?
choices: Compiled bytecode
Only NoSQL documents
Entities and their fields
Database tables and columns directly
questions.explanation: JPQL queries are written in terms of entity names and their fields (e.g. SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.age > 18), and the JPA provider translates that into the actual SQL for the underlying database.

items.title: Entity relationships
items.context: @ManyToOne / @OneToMany model one-to-many relationships (e.g. many Orders belong to one Customer). @ManyToMany models a many-to-many relationship, typically backed by a join table.

questions.prompt: Modeling "many Orders belong to one Customer", which annotation goes on the Order entity's customer field?
choices: @ManyToMany
@OneToOne
@ManyToOne
@OneToMany
questions.explanation: From the Order side, many orders point to a single customer — that's the 'many' side of the relationship, mapped with @ManyToOne.

items.title: Cascade types
items.context: CascadeType controls whether operations on a parent entity (persist, merge, remove, ...) automatically propagate to its related child entities. CascadeType.ALL applies every cascade operation, which is convenient but can unintentionally delete children you didn't mean to remove.

questions.prompt: What does CascadeType.ALL on a @OneToMany association mean?
choices: Persist, merge, remove, and other lifecycle operations on the parent automatically propagate to its children
It only applies to reads, never writes
It disables lazy loading
Child entities are ignored entirely
questions.explanation: CascadeType.ALL propagates every relevant JPA lifecycle operation from the parent to its associated children — so, for example, deleting the parent also deletes its children, which is powerful but worth using deliberately.

items.title: Optimistic locking with @Version
items.context: A @Version field (checked and incremented on every update) lets JPA detect when two transactions tried to modify the same row concurrently, throwing an OptimisticLockException on the losing update instead of silently overwriting changes.

questions.prompt: What problem does a @Version field on an entity help prevent?
choices: SQL injection
Slow query performance
Running out of database connections
Lost updates from two concurrent transactions overwriting each other's changes undetected
questions.explanation: JPA checks the version column on update; if another transaction already bumped it since this transaction read the row, the update fails with an OptimisticLockException instead of silently clobbering the other change.

items.title: Pagination & custom queries
items.context: Adding a Pageable parameter to a Spring Data repository method automatically supports paging and sorting, returning a Page<T>. For queries the derived-method-name convention can't express, @Query lets you write custom JPQL (or native SQL) directly on the repository method.

questions.prompt: Which type do you add as a repository method parameter to get automatic pagination and sorting support?
choices: QueryHint
Page
Pageable
Sort.Direction
questions.explanation: Adding a Pageable parameter (built with PageRequest.of(page, size, sort)) lets Spring Data JPA automatically apply LIMIT/OFFSET-style paging and return a Page<T> with metadata like total pages.

questions.prompt: When a query is too complex for Spring Data's method-name derivation, what lets you write it explicitly on the repository method?
choices: @Autowired
@Query, with JPQL or native SQL
@Entity
@Transactional
questions.explanation: @Query lets you attach a hand-written JPQL (or, with nativeQuery = true, raw SQL) statement directly to a repository method when the derived-query naming convention isn't expressive enough.

items.title: First-level vs second-level cache
items.context: Hibernate's first-level cache is per-EntityManager/session and always on — within one session, loading the same entity twice returns the same cached instance. The second-level cache is shared across sessions and must be explicitly enabled and configured, caching entity data across multiple transactions.

questions.prompt: What is the scope of Hibernate's first-level cache?
choices: Shared across the entire application, always
Scoped to a single database table
Scoped to a single EntityManager/session, and always active
It doesn't exist unless manually enabled
questions.explanation: The first-level cache lives inside a single persistence context (EntityManager/session) and is on by default — no configuration needed — but it disappears once that session ends.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes the second-level cache from the first-level cache?
choices: It's shared across sessions/transactions and must be explicitly enabled and configured
It replaces the need for a database entirely
It only caches primitive values, never entities
It's identical to the first-level cache
questions.explanation: Unlike the always-on, session-scoped first-level cache, the second-level cache persists entity data across multiple sessions and requires opting in (a provider like Ehcache plus explicit configuration).

items.title: Auditing entities
items.context: Spring Data JPA auditing (enabled via @EnableJpaAuditing) automatically populates fields annotated @CreatedDate, @LastModifiedDate, @CreatedBy, and @LastModifiedBy whenever an entity is persisted or updated, removing the need to set those timestamps by hand everywhere.

questions.prompt: What does Spring Data JPA auditing (@EnableJpaAuditing plus field annotations like @CreatedDate) do?
choices: Encrypts entity fields automatically
Logs every SQL statement to a file
Validates entity fields against business rules
Automatically populates creation/modification timestamp (and user) fields whenever an entity is saved or updated
questions.explanation: Once enabled, Spring Data JPA fills in @CreatedDate/@LastModifiedDate (and the *By variants, given an AuditorAware bean) automatically on persist/update, instead of every service method having to set them manually.

questions.prompt: Which annotation must be added to a configuration class to turn on JPA auditing support in the first place?
choices: @JpaAudit
@Auditable
@EnableJpaAuditing
@EnableAuditing
questions.explanation: @EnableJpaAuditing on a configuration class switches on the auditing machinery; without it, @CreatedDate/@LastModifiedDate fields are just inert annotations that never get populated.

items.title: DTO projections
items.context: Rather than returning full JPA entities from a repository, a DTO (or a Spring Data interface projection) exposes only the fields a particular use case needs — decoupling the API/response shape from the persistence model, and avoiding fetching more data than necessary.

questions.prompt: Why might you return a DTO or projection from a repository query instead of the full entity?
choices: Entities cannot be returned from repositories at all
DTOs are required by the JPA specification
It's the only way to run a query at all
To avoid exposing internal persistence details, reduce over-fetching, and decouple the API shape from the entity model
questions.explanation: Returning a purpose-built DTO/projection lets a query fetch and expose exactly the fields a use case needs, rather than the full entity (with all its associations and internal fields) every time — better performance and a cleaner API boundary.

items.title: @Embeddable value types
items.context: @Embeddable marks a class whose fields are embedded directly into the owning entity's table (via @Embedded), rather than mapped to a separate table with its own relationship — useful for value objects like an Address or Money that don't need independent identity.

questions.prompt: What does marking a class @Embeddable and using it with @Embedded in an entity achieve?
choices: Creates a separate table with a @OneToOne relationship
Enables lazy loading for that field
Embeds that class's fields directly into the owning entity's own table, with no separate identity
Makes the class immutable automatically
questions.explanation: @Embeddable value types have no identity of their own (no @Id) and their fields are folded directly into the columns of whichever entity embeds them via @Embedded — a good fit for things like Address or Money.

items.title: Batch inserts and performance
items.context: Calling repository.save() once per entity inside a loop can trigger many individual round-trips/flushes to the database. Batching (via Hibernate's batch configuration, or saveAll() with appropriate flush/clear behavior) groups multiple inserts into fewer round-trips, which matters a lot at scale.

questions.prompt: A service inserts 10,000 rows by calling repository.save(entity) once per entity inside a loop, and it's slow. What's a common way to improve this?
choices: Add more indexes to the table
Increase the connection pool size only
Use batched inserts (e.g. saveAll() with Hibernate batch settings configured, periodically flushing and clearing the persistence context)
Switch every field to lazy loading
questions.explanation: Without batching, each save() can trigger its own round-trip and the persistence context accumulates every managed entity in memory; configuring JDBC batching and periodically flushing/clearing lets many inserts go out together, dramatically reducing overhead for bulk operations.

items.title: Dynamic queries with Specifications
items.context: The JPA Criteria API (and Spring Data's Specification wrapper around it) lets you build queries programmatically and type-safely, composing filter conditions at runtime — useful when a query's shape depends on which optional filters the caller actually supplied.

questions.prompt: What problem do JPA Criteria API / Spring Data Specifications solve that derived query methods and static @Query strings don't handle well?
choices: They automatically cache every query result
They make queries run faster than JPQL
They eliminate the need for a database
They let you build queries dynamically at runtime, composing optional filter conditions programmatically
questions.explanation: Derived method names and fixed @Query strings are static; when a search endpoint has many optional filters that may or may not be applied, Specifications let you compose the WHERE conditions programmatically based on which filters were actually provided.

items.title: Orphan removal
items.context: orphanRemoval=true on a @OneToMany association tells JPA to automatically delete a child entity when it's removed from the parent's collection — even if you never explicitly called delete() on that child.

questions.prompt: What does orphanRemoval=true do on a @OneToMany relationship?
choices: Makes the association lazy instead of eager
Prevents any child entities from ever being deleted
Requires manually cascading every operation
Automatically deletes a child entity when it's removed from the parent's collection, without an explicit delete call
questions.explanation: With orphanRemoval=true, simply removing a child from the parent's collection (and flushing/committing) is enough for JPA to delete that now-'orphaned' child row — no explicit repository.delete() call needed.

items.title: Dirty checking
items.context: Hibernate tracks a snapshot of a managed entity's state when it's loaded. At flush time, it compares the entity's current state against that snapshot to figure out which fields actually changed — this 'dirty checking' is why you don't need to call an explicit update() after modifying a managed entity's fields.

questions.prompt: How does Hibernate know which fields to include in an UPDATE statement after you modify a managed entity's setters?
choices: You must call entity.markDirty() manually
It re-reads the entity from the database before every update
Dirty checking: Hibernate compares the entity's current state against a snapshot taken when it was loaded, at flush time
It always updates every column, regardless of what changed
questions.explanation: Because a managed entity's original loaded state is snapshotted, Hibernate's dirty checking can diff current vs. snapshot at flush time and generate an UPDATE for exactly the changed fields — no explicit save() call is even required for a managed entity's changes to persist.

items.title: Custom repository implementations
items.context: When a query can't be expressed by method-name derivation or JPQL/@Query, you can add a custom interface (e.g. UserRepositoryCustom) with a hand-written implementation class (UserRepositoryCustomImpl), then have the main repository interface extend both JpaRepository and the custom interface.

questions.prompt: How do you add a repository method whose logic can't be expressed via derived query methods or JPQL?
choices: Define a custom interface plus an implementation class following Spring Data's naming convention, and have the repository interface extend it
It's impossible with Spring Data repositories
Rewrite the entire repository as a plain JDBC class
Put the logic in the entity class itself
questions.explanation: Spring Data supports custom implementations: declare an extra interface (e.g. UserRepositoryCustom) with a matching *Impl class containing hand-written logic, then extend both JpaRepository and that custom interface in the main repository — Spring Data wires them together automatically.

items.title: Managed entities and the persistence context
items.context: An entity becomes "managed" once it's loaded (or persisted) within an EntityManager's persistence context — the EntityManager tracks its state and changes to it are automatically synchronized to the database on flush. Once the persistence context closes (e.g. the transaction ends), the entity becomes detached.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a JPA entity to be "managed"?
choices: It has been marked @Entity in code
It has a non-null @Id value
It implements Serializable
It's currently associated with an active persistence context, so its changes are tracked and flushed to the database automatically
questions.explanation: A managed entity is tracked by the current EntityManager/persistence context — Hibernate watches its fields for changes (dirty checking) and synchronizes them to the database at flush time, without an explicit save call.

items.title: Default fetch type per association
items.context: JPA's default fetch types differ by association: @ManyToOne and @OneToOne default to EAGER (the related entity loads immediately with its owner). @OneToMany and @ManyToMany default to LAZY (the collection loads only when accessed) — a frequently-asked, easy-to-get-wrong detail.

questions.prompt: What is the default fetch type for a @ManyToOne association, if not explicitly specified?
choices: There is no default; it must always be specified
It depends on the database vendor
LAZY
EAGER
questions.explanation: @ManyToOne (and @OneToOne) default to EAGER loading — the single related entity is fetched immediately along with its owner, unlike collection-valued associations (@OneToMany, @ManyToMany) which default to LAZY.

items.title: LazyInitializationException
items.context: Accessing a lazy-loaded association after its originating persistence context (Hibernate session) has already closed — commonly, after a @Transactional service method has returned and the entity is later touched in a view or serializer — throws LazyInitializationException, since Hibernate has nothing left to fetch the data from.

questions.prompt: A controller returns an entity fetched inside a @Transactional service method, and later code (e.g. JSON serialization) tries to access one of its lazy collections outside that transaction. What commonly happens?
choices: A compile-time error occurs
LazyInitializationException is thrown, since the persistence context/session that could have fetched the lazy data is already closed
The application silently returns an empty collection
The collection loads normally as if nothing changed
questions.explanation: Lazy associations rely on an open persistence context to fetch their data on first access; once the transaction (and its session) has ended, there's no session left to service that fetch, and Hibernate throws LazyInitializationException instead of silently doing the wrong thing.

items.title: persist() vs merge()
items.context: EntityManager.persist() takes a new, transient entity and makes it managed (schedules an INSERT). merge() instead takes a detached entity, copies its state onto a managed entity (fetching one if needed), and returns that managed copy — the original object you passed in stays detached.

questions.prompt: What's the key difference between EntityManager.persist(entity) and merge(entity)?
choices: merge() only works with new entities that have never been saved
persist() is used only for updates, merge() only for inserts
persist() makes a new transient entity managed; merge() copies a detached entity's state onto a managed instance and returns that managed copy
They are interchangeable in every case
questions.explanation: persist() is for brand-new entities becoming managed for the first time; merge() is for reattaching a detached entity's changes onto the persistence context, returning a different (managed) object than the one you passed in — the input entity itself remains detached.

items.title: Entity lifecycle states
items.context: A JPA entity moves through four states: transient (a plain new object, not yet associated with any persistence context), managed (tracked by a persistence context, changes auto-flushed), detached (was managed, but the persistence context has closed), and removed (scheduled for deletion).

questions.prompt: Which JPA entity state describes an object that was previously managed but whose persistence context has since closed?
choices: Detached
Transient
Managed
Removed
questions.explanation: Detached describes an entity that the persistence context once tracked but no longer does (e.g. after the transaction/session ended) — its data is still there, but changes to it are no longer automatically synchronized to the database.

items.title: save() vs saveAndFlush()
items.context: Spring Data's save() may defer the actual SQL INSERT/UPDATE until the persistence context's next flush (e.g. at transaction commit). saveAndFlush() forces that flush immediately, which matters when subsequent code in the same transaction needs to see the change reflected via a fresh query right away.

questions.prompt: Code calls repository.save(entity) and then immediately runs a native/JPQL query expecting to see that change, within the same transaction. Why might the query not reflect it yet?
choices: save() doesn't actually persist anything
The query is cached and never updates
save() may not flush to the database immediately; saveAndFlush() (or an explicit flush()) forces the pending change out right away
Native queries can never see JPA-managed changes
questions.explanation: save() can leave the change sitting in the persistence context until the next automatic flush point; a query that bypasses the persistence context's tracked state (like a native SQL query) may run against the database before that flush happens, unless you explicitly flush first.

items.title: @Transactional propagation
items.context: Propagation.REQUIRED (the default) joins an existing transaction if one is active, or starts a new one if not. Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW always suspends any existing transaction and starts a completely independent new one — useful when a piece of work (like audit logging) must commit regardless of whether the outer transaction later rolls back.

questions.prompt: What does @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW) do when called from within an already-active transaction?
choices: It joins the existing transaction, same as REQUIRED
It throws an exception, since nested transactions aren't allowed
It suspends the existing transaction and starts a brand-new, independent one
It has no effect on transaction behavior
questions.explanation: REQUIRES_NEW always creates a fresh, independent transaction, pausing the caller's transaction for its duration — useful when you need some work to commit (or roll back) on its own, unaffected by what happens to the outer transaction afterward.

items.title: Query by Example
items.context: Query by Example lets you build a query dynamically from a partially-populated entity instance acting as a matching template (an Example<T>), instead of writing a derived method name or JPQL for every possible combination of optional filters.

questions.prompt: What does Spring Data's Query by Example feature let you do?
choices: Build a dynamic query by passing in a partially-filled entity instance as a matching template
Generate database schema from an example row
Automatically write JPQL from SQL
Cache query results based on a sample object
questions.explanation: Query by Example wraps a partially-populated entity in an Example<T> and matches other entities against whichever fields you set, avoiding the need to hand-write a method (or Specification) for every possible combination of optional search criteria.

items.title: Sorting repository results
items.context: Adding a Sort parameter to a Spring Data repository method (alongside or instead of Pageable) lets callers specify the ordering of results without needing a dedicated derived method name for every sort combination.

questions.prompt: Which type can you add as a repository method parameter to control the ordering of results without a separate method per sort order?
choices: Comparator
IndexedSort
Sort
Order
questions.explanation: Passing a Sort instance (e.g. Sort.by("lastName").ascending()) as a method parameter lets Spring Data apply that ordering to the query dynamically, instead of needing separate methods like findAllByOrderByLastNameAsc().

items.title: flush() vs commit()
items.context: flush() synchronizes the persistence context's pending changes to the database (running the actual SQL) without ending the transaction — the changes are visible to other queries in the same transaction/connection, but not yet permanent. commit() ends the transaction, making those changes permanent (or rolling everything back if something failed).

questions.prompt: What does calling flush() on an EntityManager do that commit() does not?
choices: They are exactly the same operation
flush() only works on read-only transactions
flush() ends the transaction; commit() does not
flush() pushes pending changes to the database as SQL without ending the transaction; commit() ends the transaction, making changes permanent
questions.explanation: flush() forces the persistence context to send its pending SQL to the database right now — useful when you need the DB state to reflect changes mid-transaction — while the transaction itself remains open until an explicit commit (or rollback) later.

items.title: Batch fetching configuration
items.context: Hibernate's batch-fetch size setting (hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size, or @BatchSize on an association) groups multiple pending lazy-association fetches into fewer, larger IN-clause queries instead of one query per parent — reducing (though not fully eliminating) the N+1 query problem.

questions.prompt: How does configuring a Hibernate batch-fetch size help with the N+1 problem?
choices: It forces every association to load eagerly
It groups multiple pending lazy fetches into fewer batched queries (e.g. using an IN clause) instead of one query per parent entity
It only affects native SQL queries, not JPQL
It eliminates lazy loading entirely
questions.explanation: Instead of firing one query per parent entity's lazy association (true N+1), batch fetching groups several of those pending lookups together into a single query using an IN clause — cutting the number of round-trips even though it doesn't fully collapse everything into one query like a JOIN FETCH would.

items.title: LazyInitializationException outside a session

questions.prompt: What happens on author.books.size()?
choices: Returns 0 always for lazy collections
Triggers a new database query transparently, regardless of session state
Throws LazyInitializationException — no Hibernate Session is open anymore
Prints the number of books normally
questions.explanation: The @Transactional method returns, closing the Hibernate Session/persistence context along with it. `books` was never actually loaded — only a lazy proxy was attached. Accessing it afterward, with no open session available to run the SELECT, throws LazyInitializationException ("could not initialize proxy - no Session"). Fixes include fetching eagerly, using a join-fetch query, or accessing the collection while the session is still open.

items.title: The N+1 select problem

questions.prompt: How many SQL queries does this loop typically execute?
choices: 0 — Hibernate caches everything after the first author
Exactly 2, regardless of how many authors there are
Exactly 1 — findAll() eagerly loads everything it needs
1 (for findAll) + 1 more per author to lazily load their books — the N+1 problem
questions.explanation: findAll() issues one SELECT for the 50 authors. Because `books` is lazy, each call to a.getBooks() inside the loop triggers its own separate SELECT the first time it's accessed — 50 more queries. This 1-query-plus-one-per-row pattern is the textbook N+1 problem, typically fixed with a JOIN FETCH query or a batch-fetch-size configuration.

items.title: persist() vs merge() on an existing id

questions.prompt: What happens when persist() runs, given a row with id=42 already exists?
choices: Updates the existing row with the new name
Creates a second row with the same id
Throws an exception — persist() is for creating new entities, not for ones with an already-assigned identifier for a generated-id strategy
Silently does nothing
questions.explanation: persist() is specifically for making a new, transient entity managed and eventually INSERTed — it's not the same as merge(), which is for reconciling a detached entity (possibly representing an existing row) back into the persistence context. Calling persist() on an entity whose id already corresponds to an existing row (particularly with an IDENTITY/AUTO generator that expects to assign the id itself) typically throws a PersistenceException/EntityExistsException rather than performing an update — you want merge() or save() (Spring Data's wrapper, which picks insert vs. update for you) instead.

items.title: @Transactional(readOnly = true) silently dropping writes

questions.prompt: Is the name change actually saved to the database?
choices: Only if @Modifying is also present
No — readOnly=true typically sets Hibernate's flush mode to MANUAL, so dirty-checking never flushes this change to the database
Yes — any change to a managed entity is flushed at commit regardless of readOnly
It throws TransactionRequiredException immediately when setName() is called
questions.explanation: readOnly = true is a hint that Hibernate (and other providers) commonly use to switch the session's flush mode to MANUAL and skip dirty-checking for performance — since you promised not to write anything. The entity's field is changed in memory, the method returns with no error, but nothing is ever flushed to the database, so the update is silently lost. This is a subtle bug: no exception, just a change that quietly doesn't persist.

items.title: Unique constraint violation via Spring Data

questions.prompt: What happens on the second save()?
choices: Throws DataIntegrityViolationException wrapping the unique constraint violation
The second save silently updates the first row
Both save successfully with different ids
Throws EntityExistsException
questions.explanation: The database-level unique constraint on email rejects the second row at flush time. Spring Data's exception translation converts the underlying SQL integrity-constraint exception into Spring's own DataAccessException hierarchy — specifically DataIntegrityViolationException — so calling code doesn't need to know which specific database or driver is underneath.

items.title: equals()/hashCode() on an unassigned JPA id

questions.prompt: What does this print?
choices: Throws ConcurrentModificationException
Compile error
true — it's the same object reference
false, in general — o's hashCode changed after persist() assigned its id, so HashSet is now looking in the wrong bucket
questions.explanation: o was added to the HashSet while id (and therefore hashCode()) was null, placing it in the bucket for that hash. persist() then mutates o.id, which changes hashCode() out from under the already-placed entry — but HashSet doesn't re-bucket existing entries when their hash changes. A later contains(o), computed with the *new* hash, looks in the wrong bucket and typically returns false. This is a well-known JPA pitfall: basing equals()/hashCode() on a generated id that isn't stable until persist().

items.title: orphanRemoval automatically deleting a child

questions.prompt: What happens to that removed LineItem row in the database?
choices: It's only removed if cascade = CascadeType.REMOVE is also present
It throws an exception, since the item was never explicitly deleted via the repository
Nothing — removing from a List is purely in-memory and doesn't touch the database
It's automatically DELETEd from the database at flush time, because of orphanRemoval = true
questions.explanation: orphanRemoval = true tells Hibernate to treat "no longer referenced by its parent's collection" as equivalent to "should be deleted" — simply removing the LineItem from order.getItems() and letting the transaction commit is enough to trigger a DELETE for that row, no explicit repository call needed. Without orphanRemoval, the same removal would just detach the association (nulling the FK, if nullable) but leave the row in the database.

items.title: Updating only the inverse (mappedBy) side

questions.prompt: Does this persist a link between order 5 and customer 1?
choices: Yes — JPA keeps both sides of a bidirectional relationship in sync automatically
Yes, but only after calling flush() explicitly
It throws an exception for updating only one side
No — the foreign key lives on the owning (@ManyToOne) side, and only o.setCustomer(c) actually updates it; mutating the mappedBy collection alone has no effect on the database
questions.explanation: In a bidirectional @OneToMany/@ManyToOne mapping, the @ManyToOne side owns the relationship — its column is the actual foreign key that gets written to the database. The mappedBy side is purely a convenience view for navigating in Java; Hibernate doesn't inspect it when deciding what SQL to issue. Adding `o` to `c.getOrders()` changes an in-memory List and nothing else — you must also call `o.setCustomer(c)` for the FK to actually update.

items.title: First-level cache returning the same reference

questions.prompt: What does this print, assuming both calls happen inside the same transaction/persistence context?
choices: Throws an exception on the second find()
It depends on whether the entity has a @Version field
true — the persistence context's first-level cache returns the exact same managed instance for the same id without a second query
false — find() always queries the database and builds a new object
questions.explanation: Every persistence context (EntityManager) maintains a first-level cache keyed by entity type + id. The first find() queries the database and registers the resulting managed entity in that cache; the second find() for the same id, within the same context, returns that cached object directly — no second SQL query, and crucially, `==` reference equality holds, not just equals().

items.title: remove() on a detached entity

questions.prompt: What happens when delete() is called on a detached entity, depending on the provider/version?
choices: It always works fine — Spring Data re-attaches detached entities transparently in every case
It throws LazyInitializationException
It silently does nothing
It can throw IllegalArgumentException ("Removing a detached instance") because remove() generally requires a managed entity
questions.explanation: EntityManager.remove() (which Spring Data's delete() delegates to) generally expects a managed entity — one that's currently tracked by an active persistence context. Calling it on a detached instance (loaded, then the session/context ended) is a classic source of IllegalArgumentException. Spring Data repositories often re-fetch or merge before deleting specifically to avoid this trap, but the underlying JPA contract still requires managed state for remove().
